Participants could select more than one option in each section. 434 435 Qualitative findings illustrated how these benefits supported day-to-day work. Participants described 436 task reminders as helping them plan upcoming visits and prepare required medicines and other 437 commodities, while longitudinal participant records facilitated access to information from previous 438 encounters and reduced reliance on paper records that could be lost. Participants also linked the clinical 439 guidance provided by the application to greater confidence and credibility with patients. Beyond these 440 direct functions, some described digital documentation as strengthening accountability by making 441 completed work traceable: 442 "Without CHT I think our work would lack credibility, there was going to be a lot of cheating but with 443 CHT there is no chance of cheating." (FGD, Butha-Buthe) 444 Another participant similarly contrasted the application with paper-based reporting, where tasks could 445 be recorded as completed without necessarily having been performed. While supervisory visibility was 446 frequently perceived positively, 6 (6%) CHWs identified supervisors being able to check entered data as 447 a challenge and 5 (5%) reported data-privacy concerns (Table 4). Qualitative accounts also showed that 448 task visibility could have unintended consequences when completion depended on participant availability: one participant noted that tasks remaining pending could make it appear that the CHW was not doing the work.

The most frequently reported challenges were long questionnaires (64%), difficulty charging tablets (49%), and limited internet connectivity (33%). Qualitative accounts indicated that much of the questionnaire burden related to research-specific consent and baseline data collection rather than the clinical care workflows themselves. Some participants described these questions as lengthy or intrusive.

Charging difficulties were particularly relevant in villages without electricity, while poor network connectivity primarily affected synchronization. Participants also described occasional tensions between following standardized decision support and responding to situations in which the application's recommendation did not align with their expectations or with care provided elsewhere.

That causes a lot of confusion because as a person you would also want to work the way you were trained. But at the end of the day CHT forces you to do what it says." (IDI, female CHW, Butha-Buthe) The participant clarified that this did not occur often but described situations in which the algorithm's recommendation differed from subsequent facility treatment. A related tension arose when the algorithm recommended reducing or discontinuing antihypertensive medication. Participants described difficulty explaining this to patients who understood antihypertensive treatment to be lifelong: "...some of the patients do not trust what we say to them because they have an old information that when you are on this kind of treatment you are not to stop taking medication." (FGD, Mokhotlong)

The same participant suggested that confirmation from a facility nurse could help patients accept such treatment changes. In one interview, a CHW also described having become reliant on the application's confirmation when diagnosing hypertension and type 2 diabetes, illustrating that decision support could increase confidence while potentially creating dependence on the system.

Participants also identified challenges related to information continuity across care providers. They described patients using multiple personal health booklets, treatment changes made at health facilities that were not always known to the CHW, and medication obtained from multiple sources, creating a potential risk of duplication.

"A challenge of clients who mix pills or overdose because they will be taking medication from me and when the outreach is there, they also go there and get medication." (FGD, Butha-Buthe) Suggested improvements included a better overview of households and participants (50%), automated SMS reminders for participants (47%), fewer questions (33%), and greater flexibility in scheduling tasks (24%). The qualitative findings supported the desire for greater scheduling flexibility: participants valued automated task reminders but described situations in which predefined task timing did not align with participant availability, and some suggested being able to schedule their own visits while retaining supervisory visibility. Although SMS reminders were among the most requested additions, qualitative accounts revealed divergent views. Some participants considered SMS useful for reminding participants of upcoming visits, whereas others raised concerns about limited phone ownership, low literacy, confidentiality on shared phones, and potential family conflict or safety concerns: "Most of our patients don't have phones, they share phones. Imagine now sending a text message, it is going to raise a lot of suspicions." (FGD, Mokhotlong)

The broader discussion in the same FGD included concerns about disclosure of illness to family members and potential conflict arising from messages sent between CHWs and participants. One interview participant suggested telephone calls as a preferable alternative for some participants. Additional suggestions arising from the qualitative data included enabling consultation with supervisors directly within the application, extending digital workflows to health facilities and routine Ministry of Health reporting, and broadening the platform to additional community health services such as HIV testing and family planning.

Discussion

.

In this mixed-methods evaluation among all 103 CHWs delivering community-based hypertension and type 2 diabetes care in rural Lesotho, the ComBaCaL application was highly usable and valued by its users. CHWs rated both the general application functions, such as participant registration and overview, task management and reporting, and the more demanding clinical tasks of diagnosis and treatment as easy, while most reported these would be harder to perform without the application. The qualitative findings extended the survey results: usability developed through experience and was sustained by training and supervision, and CHWs described tensions around standardization, operational flexibility, accountability, and continuity of care between community and facility levels. Together with the three nested cluster-randomized trials, which provided clinical evidence for the broader CHW-led care models, this study provides an additional, user-centered account of how the underlying application was experienced [24] [25] [26].

Digital CDSSs have enabled several task-shared models of non-communicable disease care, but in almost all of them the authority to initiate and adjust treatment has remained with a professional cadre rather than the CHW [38]. In SMARThealth India, CHWs conducted tablet-based cardiovascular risk assessment and referral while the decision support and treatment decisions were directed to primary-care physicians [39]. In more recent work in Kenya and Uganda, CHWs facilitated home-based hypertension care, but titration was clinician-driven through telehealth [40], and in Guatemala CHWs used a smartphone application to screen for and diagnose hypertension and diabetes, with treatment adjustment made by a healthcare professional [41, 42]. While mWellcare, a tablet-based system for integrated hypertension and diabetes management, delivered a comparably broad care support, it was nurse-led rather than delivered by lay workers [43]. The ComBaCaL model extends this experience by enabling CHWs themselves to deliver the full longitudinal pathway at community level -diagnosis, independent treatment initiation and titration, cardiovascular risk management, referral and repeated follow-up.

The good overall usability, reflected in a mean SUS score of 75.6, above the commonly cited benchmark of 68 [30], is notable given the clinical and longitudinal complexity of the application. The common interface, longitudinal records, task management, and offline-first architecture were provided by the established CHT Core Framework, while ComBaCaL-specific workflows and clinical decision support were configured within it. The observed usability therefore reflects the combination of the underlying framework, application configuration, and the training and supervision provided, consistent with evidence that enabling conditions are important for health workers' adoption of digital technologies in low-and middle-income settings [44]. At the item level, responses were strongly favorable for integration and confidence, while learnability items were more mixed, corresponding with qualitative accounts of initial difficulty followed by increasing confidence with practice. Responses to the single reverse-worded item on inconsistency were a notable exception: only a minority responded favorably, despite near-universal agreement that the application's functions were well integrated. This most likely reflects variable interpretation due to lack of a specific term in Sesotho rather than genuinely inconsistent performance.

The use of CHT is also relevant to the potential for wider implementation. Rather than developing a stand-alone application specifically for this project, the ComBaCaL workflows were configured within an open-source framework designed for reuse and large-scale deployment and already used in large-scale and national community health programs in multiple countries [14]. This does not establish the scalability or sustainability of the ComBaCaL application itself, but it provides an established technical foundation on which the application can be adapted and extended without rebuilding the underlying architecture.

Beyond overall usability, the findings illustrate how the application supported the longitudinal demands of chronic care. Most CHWs reported that diagnosis and treatment would be more difficult without the application, and qualitative accounts linked this support to step-by-step guidance, safeguards, access to information from previous encounters, and task reminders. The workflow carried information forward between visits and adapted the next recommended action as clinical status, treatment uptake, medication availability, participant preferences, or referral needs changed over time. This allowed screening, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up to be managed within a single longitudinal pathway.

Taken together, the findings suggest that this degree of clinical and longitudinal complexity remained manageable for CHWs, while the study cannot isolate the application's contribution from training, supervision, medication supply, and other components of the care model.

The strongly positive assessments were accompanied by tensions between standardization and flexibility. Operationally, some CHWs wanted greater control over task timing when participants were unavailable, suggesting that structured follow-up schedules need sufficient flexibility to accommodate circumstances outside the CHW's control. Clinically, however, standardization remained important, particularly because CHWs were undertaking tasks such as treatment initiation and adjustment.

Participants occasionally described recommendations that were difficult to reconcile with care provided elsewhere or with patients' expectations, particularly when protocol-defined blood-pressure thresholds led to reduction or discontinuation of antihypertensive treatment. These accounts highlight the importance of clear communication across providers, accessible supervision and escalation pathways, and training for CHWs in explaining guideline-based treatment decisions to patients. One participant also reflected on becoming reliant on the application's confirmation when making decisions; although a single account, it underlines the importance of maintaining CHWs' clinical knowledge and supervisory support alongside digital guidance, so that decision support augments rather than replaces clinical judgment.

A further theme was accountability. Some participants described the application as lending credibility to their work with patients and colleagues and as ensuring scheduled tasks were genuinely carried out rather than only recorded as complete, suggesting digital decision support may strengthen not only the consistency of care but also its perceived legitimacy and supervision. This visibility was not universally welcomed: a minority saw supervisory oversight as a drawback (6%) or raised data-privacy concerns (5%), and one participant noted that tasks left pending because a participant could not be reached might make it appear the CHW had not worked. Digital traceability can thus strengthen supervision, but performance monitoring must distinguish non-completion attributable to the CHW from tasks unresolved for reasons beyond their control.

Several practical challenges are relevant for wider implementation. The most frequently reported challenge of lengthy questionnaires was attributed qualitatively to research-specific consent and baseline data collection rather than the clinical workflows, so the burden seen here likely overstates that of a platform used primarily for routine care. Charging and intermittent connectivity remained relevant despite offline-first functionality. Although SMS reminders to participants were among the most requested additions, CHWs themselves raised confidentiality and safety concerns about messaging participants on shared phones, illustrating the value of involving frontline users before adding features that may carry social risks. More broadly, these experiences underscore the value of involving frontline CHWs in the ongoing development and adaptation of routine decision-support tools for noncommunicable diseases in Lesotho, so that usability and contextual challenges are addressed before wider rollout.

Information continuity across care providers emerged as an additional challenge. Participants described treatment changes that were not always known to CHWs and medication obtained from multiple sources, which could complicate medication reconciliation and create a risk of duplication. These challenges are not specific to the application and would not be fully resolved by digital integration alone, as information on care received elsewhere may remain incomplete and clinical history-taking also relies on patient-reported information. Nevertheless, extending digital workflows across community and facility levels could improve access to shared longitudinal information and reduce avoidable gaps in communication and parallel documentation.

The study has several strengths. All 103 CHWs completed the survey, giving complete coverage and minimizing non-response bias, and the mixed-methods design allowed survey findings to be contextualized and, at times, challenged by qualitative accounts. Notably, the qualitative component elicited criticisms and tensions as well as positive assessments, indicating participants were willing to voice concerns and offering some reassurance against uniformly positive reporting. The evaluation also followed sustained use across 103 villages and three cluster-randomized trials, reflecting repeated field use of a mature application rather than first impressions from a small pilot.

Several limitations apply. The study was conducted within a single research implementation in rural Lesotho, which may limit transferability. Participating CHWs were relatively young and probably more educated than the current national workforce. However, villages were selected independently of CHW characteristics, and replacement CHWs were identified according to Ministry of Health procedures rather than preferentially selected for digital skills. Participants themselves questioned whether older or less-educated CHWs would find the application as usable, and usability may differ in settings with less training, supervision, or infrastructure. Social-desirability bias may have inflated favorable responses, as participants knew the study team had developed the application, although IDIs and FGDs were conducted by a researcher not involved in delivery and the data included criticism. Some survey items used predefined categories that may not capture all experiences; the study assessed perceptions rather than objective performance or diagnostic accuracy and cannot isolate the application's independent contribution to the trial outcomes. Finally, we did not evaluate the scalability or long-term sustainability of the application itself; the arrangements that routine implementation at scale would require are discussed above.

Conclusion

The ComBaCaL application was highly usable and valued by CHWs delivering longitudinal hypertension and diabetes care in rural Lesotho, with usability extending from general application functions to complex clinical workflows spanning diagnosis, treatment, medication management and repeated follow-up. This supports the suitability of the open-source CHT Core Framework for complex longitudinal chronic-care applications in this setting and suggests that, with appropriate workflow design, training, supervision and infrastructure, digital decision support can help CHWs deliver guideline-based chronic care. With the clinical evidence from the ComBaCaL trials, these findings support digitally enabled community-based chronic care, including independent first-line medication management, while identifying operational flexibility and integration across health-system levels as priorities for wider implementation.

S1 Appendix. Survey instrument.

Full quantitative survey administered to all 103 community health workers, presented in both English and Sesotho. The instrument covers demographic characteristics, educational attainment, English proficiency, and prior digital experience; the System Usability Scale; items on perceived usefulness, satisfaction, and perceived value adapted from the mHealth App Usability Questionnaire (MAUQ) and the Primary Care Information Project Provider Survey; task-specific ease-of-use items adapted from the Single Ease Question approach; and study-specific items on perceived benefits, challenges, and recommendations for future implementation.

S2 Fig.

Diabetes screening and diagnosis algorithm for people not reporting use of antidiabetic medication. FBG: fasting blood glucose; RBG: random blood glucose. Capillary blood was used for all measurements. Measurements were considered fasting blood glucose if participants reported no caloric intake in the eight hours before the measurement; all other measurements were considered random blood glucose. Type 2 diabetes was defined as (1) self-reported use of antidiabetic medication; (2) an FBG ≥ 7 mmol/l or an RBG ≥ 11.1 mmol/l after a previously elevated FBG or RBG ≥ 5.6 mmol/l; or (3) an FBG ≥ 7 mmol/l or an RBG ≥ 11.1 mmol/l in the presence of all three cardinal symptoms of uncontrolled diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss) in the absence of a clinical history suggestive of type 1 diabetes.

S3 Fig. Hypertension treatment algorithm applied by community health workers in the intervention villages.

HCTz: hydrochlorothiazide; SBP: systolic blood pressure; DBP: diastolic blood pressure; CVD: cardiovascular disease. ¹De-escalation only if SBP < 120 mmHg and DBP < 90 mmHg. At every visit, the community health worker (CHW) documented current medication, adherence, and blood pressure values. Measurements were taken after selecting the appropriate cuff size, with participants seated after at least five minutes of rest. At the initial visit, blood pressure was measured in both arms, and subsequent measurements were taken from the arm with the higher systolic pressure. The blood pressure value was calculated as the mean of the last two of three consecutive measurements obtained at one-minute intervals. If no contraindications were present, CHWs offered a fixed-dose combination pill containing amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide, with titration according to the algorithm of the Lesotho Standard Treatment Guidelines. Participants with a blood pressure ≥ 140/90 mmHg under highdose amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide, those with contraindications or intolerance to amlodipine/hydrochlorothiazide, and those refusing the medications offered by the CHW were referred to the closest health facility. Treatment was discontinued or de-intensified if systolic blood pressure was < 120 mmHg and diastolic blood pressure was < 90 mmHg. Follow-up visits were scheduled after one month if the dose was adjusted during the index visit, or after two months if the dose was not adjusted. Participants with high CVD risk and no contraindications were offered atorvastatin 10 mg daily. High CVD risk among people with hypertension was defined as a history of stroke or myocardial infarction; diabetes or chronic kidney disease; or being ≥ 50 years old and currently smoking or having a BMI ≥ 30 kg/m². Participants with a history of myocardial infarction or stroke were offered acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) 100 mg daily. Participants not already taking metformin, not meeting referral criteria, and without contraindications were offered metformin initiation at 500 mg/day, with weekly titration to a maximum dose of 2 g/day.

In the case of an FBG or RBG < 4.4 mmol/l, the metformin dose was reduced by 500 mg/day. Participants with an FBG > 8.0 mmol/l or an RBG > 9.9 mmol/l who reported good adherence to the maximum metformin dose were referred to the closest health facility for further management. For participants with complicated diabetes, those fulfilling referral criteria, or those with contraindications to metformin, the CDSS prompted CHWs to consult a healthcare professional to guide treatment initiation. Four participants had previous experience working as CHWs before the introduction of the digital system and were therefore able to reflect on differences between paper-based and digital workflows.Semi-structured interview guides explored experiences using the application, perceived benefits and challenges, training and support needs, usability, and the role of the application in supporting delivery of hypertension and diabetes care. The guides were pilot-tested before data collection. IDIs and FGDs were conducted in Sesotho by Motlalentoa Moruthoane, BSc Social Sciences, a male trained qualitative research assistant with previous experience conducting qualitative interviews and FGDs. He was not involved in delivering the intervention or supervising participating CHWs. Participants were informed of his role and the purpose of the qualitative study before data collection. IDIs and FGDs were conducted at the training venue, with only the researcher and participants present, and lasted approximately 30-40 and 90-100 minutes, respectively. Sessions were audio-recorded and translated into English during transcription. No repeat interviews were conducted and no field notes were taken. Transcripts were not returned to participants for comment or correction, and formal participant checking of the findings was not undertaken. The semi-structured guide for IDIs and FGDs is available in Supporting Information (S2 Appendix).

By the time of the evaluation, the application had been used to register 5283 households and 16297 participants, screen 8096 adults for hypertension and 6135 adults for type 2 diabetes, and support longitudinal care for 401 347 participants with hypertension and 60 participants with type 2 diabetes enrolled in the nested cluster-348 randomized trials.
